items.title: SN release: embedded wallet, wallet onboarding on signup, toggle receive proxy
items.text:
## first embedded wallet

We've added an ***optional*** and embedded (*ducks*) Spark wallet. For existing stackers, you can add one (or many) to your account by visiting [wallets](https://stacker.news/wallets), clicking Spark, and once it generates and tests the mnemonic, hitting save. For new stackers, they'll be presented with a "Do you need a lightning wallet?" dialog. When they select "Yes," we give them a passphrase, generate this wallet for them and add it to their account. Otherwise, and in addition, they can attach external wallets as we're already familiar with.

![](https://m.stacker.news/153885)

As much as we can, we surface the tradeoffs that one accepts by using this embedded wallet. In our opinion, people should treat it like they would a custodial wallet: when they are okay with trusting a third party with their wallet's privacy and access to their funds. Hence, if you are using our embedded Spark wallet, *treat it like a custodial wallet*:

1. Do NOT store more money in it than you can afford to lose
2. If your financial privacy needs are high, do NOT use it

![](https://m.stacker.news/153886)

We've been testing it for a few weeks ourselves and the experience is (above excluded) comparable to our attached wallets. It is bound to have some quirks though, so if you end up giving it a spin, please make us aware of any bugs/errors you encounter.

#### more embedded wallets will follow

When the technology is ready, we plan to add other embeddable wallets to SN: Ark, Lexe, I know Shocknet is working on theirs, ecash, etc. Our goal is to provide a wide range of choice because great lightning wallets, and imo embeddable wallet sdks, are important to bitcoin succeeding as an MoE (which imo requires bitcoin being used for weird things like SN where fiat is impractical).

## toggle wallet receive proxy

You can turn off the receive proxy for your lightning address now from [/settings/wallets](https://stacker.news/settings/wallets), and toggle it on/off when you generate invoices manually from a wallet. Additionally:

1. proxying receives now carries a 3% fee, down from 10%
2. even with proxying disabled, you will receive notifications about receiving money through your attached wallet on SN (if your wallet supports receive verification)
3. un-proxied receives now support lnurl comments and nostr zap receipts
   1. meaning, if you have proxying disabled on your wallets you should be able to reliably receive lnurl dms again (you can also receive them with proxying on ... if the sender doesn't send from reward sats ... I know it's complicated)

## nostr zap fixes

For many months now, we've had a bug in our nostr zap receipts that (should've) caused some clients to deem them invalid. This has been fixed along with this other work.

***

That's most of it.

Sox has been working on updating our frontend stack so we can refresh our design and do some other fun things with the UI.

As a little fun break from this harder wallet stuff, I'm going to see if I can add an optional setting allowing folks to disable receiving CCs (failing lightning zaps will fallback to donations made to the rewards pool instead), which will be a kind of pilot for potentially removing CCs at some point in the future.

items.title: Swing and a miss: Paying with Bitcoin on a Square Terminal
items.text:
This year, I've got my kids doing a homeschool co-op two days a week. This just means that a group of homeschool parents have organized to teach their children in a group setting, and possibly hire a teacher or two for subjects where more formal education might be helpful (languages, music, science?). 

Unfortunately, the coop we have joined is quite some way from our home, so after dropping off the children, I go to a nearby coffee shop to work -- a coffee shop that has a Square terminal.

I have asked if they accept Bitcoin a number of times so far, but in all cases the cashier's answer has been "I don't think so" or "I'll have to talk to the person who manages this" (pointing at the terminal). It's a busy place and so there is often a line, and I haven't wanted to try to make anyone wait while I help figure out how to turn on Bitcoin payments, and so I haven't made much progress. 

Today, the person behind the cash register was the owner and I seized my opportunity. 

I placed my order and while he was ringing it up, I said, "I've heard that these Square terminals accept bitcoin."

The owner glanced up at me and said, "I've heard that, too. Let's see if we can figure it out."

This was a much more enthusiastic response than I was expecting. He poked away at the terminal for a few minutes and then said, "I think it only takes bitcoin if you have CashApp."

I told him that this was not the case, but that if he could get it to display a QR code I could try paying that.

He continued to tap on the terminal without much effect. I should say this terminal was not the sort that has a rotatable screen. There is one fixed screen facing the cashier and a smaller fixed screen facing the customer. This was showing the message "Waiting for cashier..."

"I think you have to tap to pay," he said.

Now, I don't use any of the Lightning wallets that have implemented tap to pay (as far as I remember there aren't very many) so that wasn't an option. I told him that I needed a QR code to scan.

After another couple minutes, the owner volunteered: "Maybe I can text it to you." 

I am usually loathe to provide a phone number, but in the interest of dismantling the legacy financial system, I gave it to him. I immediately received a text with a link. The link was to pay for my coffee, but had required fields for name, phone number, and email. At the bottom I saw a green button that said pay with CashApp or something like that. I tapped it, but nothing happened because I had not entered the required fields. 

Still in the interest of taking down the fiat empire, I entered some incorrect information in these fields. But then when I tapped the green button, it presented me with a message informing me that I did not have CashApp and a button to download CashApp. 

At this point the line behind me was long enough that I offered to pay with cash and the owner accept with some visible signs of relief.

So: I have failed on this the fourth time I've tried to pay with Bitcoin at this Square terminal. I suspect that the owner needs to turn Bitcoin payments on and that I will need to talk him through this process, so I'll have to rewatch those videos about how to do this. 

It occurs to me that Square could do a lot better with this flow if they had a button that allowed the cashier to display a QR code that was simultaneously a CashApp code and a Lightning invoice. This is a lot to ask, but I'm pretty sure it needs to be at least that easy for it to work well.

items.title: Guilty until proven innocent
items.text:
ALL surveillance and control, all AML, KYC and all violations of privacy are completely unethical, immoral and illegitimate. All of them! As recently as the 1990s, one could purchase stocks without providing identification. Bank deposits below arbitrary thresholds required no explanation or documentation. Cash transactions, regardless of size, were presumed legitimate unless specific evidence suggested otherwise. The default assumption was that individuals had the right to conduct their financial affairs privately, with the burden of proof resting on authorities to demonstrate wrongdoing before intruding upon that privacy.

This historical norm was not an oversight or a failure of governance, it was a recognition of a fundamental principle. Free societies operate on the presumption of innocence, treating citizens as autonomous agents capable of managing their own affairs unless proven otherwise through due process. The current system inverts this relationship entirely, treating every citizen as a potential criminal whose financial activities must be continuously monitored and pre-approved by state bureaucrats. Given how KYC for everything short of going to a rest room is being normalized, the world needs more privacy protecting tools, not less.

items.title: Is L-BTC a shitcoin?
items.text:
# The closest I've ever come to being a shitcoiner

Back in 2024, I spent a lot of time looking at ecash. Ecash is cool -- it has all these neat properties like potentially better privacy and maybe being a bearer asset like cash and being so lightweight that almost anyone can run a mint and cypherpunks have been working on ecash since long before bitcoin. Development in Cashu and Fedimint was in full flower and there weren't many viable alternatives like Ark or Spark.

@TonyGiorgio wrote a post in January of 2024 called "Fedimint is Self-Custodial" https://stacker.news/items/395461 which was the catalyst for a particular fascination of mine: trying to determine what sort of thing an ecash token actually is. Is it like a gift card? https://stacker.news/items/397764/r/Scoresby or a repurchase agreement a la the Fed's repo window? https://stacker.news/items/565172/r/Scoresby Is it a token you buy? https://stacker.news/items/554143/r/Scoresby

It was clear to me that ecash tokens were not bitcoin, but at that point in Bitcoin culture if a token wasn't bitcoin, it could only be a shitcoin -- and yet I didn't think using ecash was shitcoining. I think this was because I associate shitcoining with scamming and degenerate trading and pump 'n dump schemes while ecash was clearly trying to do payments.

I got so interested in the idea that I believe @Car felt compelled to block me and I recall a number of fiery conversations with @justin_shocknet.

# Justin was right

There were many points about which we disagreed, but I believe one of the most significant was that I tried to defend the use of ecash as less trusting than simply relying on a custodian. About this, I was most certainly wrong. Here is Justin [explaining it to me](https://stacker.news/items/554143/r/Scoresby?commentId=554230):

![](https://m.stacker.news/155829)

# Why the change of mind

That last bit in Justin's comment gets at it. I wanted to think about a mint in isolation or as a complete system, but this is obviously not the case. Ecash mints are an attempt to glue a non-bitcoin system onto bitcoin and so evaluating as some whole thing on its own was not particularly relevant to users who were interested in sats.

This was made painfully clear by the recent Liquid hack. There are 15 "geographically distributed" Liquid functionaries in their federation and at least 11 of them are required to finalize blocks. And yet, almost the entire amount of bitcoin in the Liquid Network was withdrawn and block production was halted.

In that moment, calling a Liquid wallet self-custodial was pretty clearly demonstrated to be wrong. If you have a L-BTC balance in ACQUA Wallet, Manna Wallet, or Misty Breez you can't move your sats (and you may not actually have any sats). Doesn't sound very self-custodial.

This interaction with @Roy_Breez was very enlightening:

![](https://imgprxy.stacker.news/Uv9piRjMpEGZXhf394gOtE-JsUrOj3DSE49enKKft_8/rs:fit:2560:1440/aHR0cHM6Ly9tLnN0YWNrZXIubmV3cy8xNTU3ODU)

![](https://imgprxy.stacker.news/Nen5MnjrhiSPdtgEtJxk1bsSkcl-edx0-smACu0JfwQ/rs:fit:2560:1440/aHR0cHM6Ly9tLnN0YWNrZXIubmV3cy8xNTU3ODY)

We've been calling these things self-custodial, but the users can't use their money and possibly don't even have it any more.

# Okay, but Coldcard users also lost funds out of their wallets...

This may seem like a pedantic point, but it really drove it home for me. The key difference between Coldcard users and Liquid users that makes one self-custodial and the other custodial is that when you open a Liquid-based wallet right now, it still shows your balance...you just don't have it. Both Coldcard users and Liquid users have experienced theft -- but the latter still have their L-BTC and that makes all the difference. Because what value does L-BTC have if there's no BTC in the Liquid Federation wallet? (or even if there's not enough BTC there?)

I wanted to be able to call things like ecash tokens and L-BTC something other than a shitcoin because I thought there was a way for them to be used in lieu of bitcoin, but the reality is that such an approach muddies the water. If we are going to call a bitcoin wallet self-custodial, the bitcoin wallet shouldn't show you a balance when there isn't one.[^1]

# Where does this leave me and my fascination with ecash and other fake L2s?

I don't think L-BTC is a shitcoin. But it ***is*** more accurate to call Liquid *custodial*. Same goes for ecash, Ark, Spark, and all the other fake L2s.

[^1]: And for you jerks who will observe that a bitcoin node that is not yet updated could also display a balance that isn't there, go look at Bitcoin Core: they have a pretty big warning that says your balance may not be accurate when you aren't synced to the current chaintip.

But this in turn has made it clear how much I need a better subscription page for SN. When I do have time for SN, I hit my subscription page and it’s fucking overwhelming. If I’m lucky, I can see maybe twelve hours worth of stuff, but sometimes, it’s only a few hours.

I subscribe to maybe eight territories, and maybe as many individual posters. But that’s enough (especially as some of the territories have gotten busier) to completely overwhelm my feed. I’ve missed plenty of important posts ([one costing me 10K sats](https://stacker.news/items/1571441) [^1]), and plenty more where I’d have loved to contributed to discussions.

One obvious solution would be to just reduce what I subscribe to. But that’s self-defeating. I subscribe to people and communities because I like them and want updates. I also (obviously) want notifications on posts I make and when I’m tagged.

What I’d like (and I have no idea if this is on the radar, nor if it’s easy/possible) is the ability to break up my subscription page. The aggregate page is fine when I’m on a lot. But when I’m not, allow me to see territory subscriptions from separately from the user subscriptions separately from the comments on my actual posts. I could manually just change all my settings each time, but if I had the time to do all that all the time, I’d have the time to keep up with my feeds. As it stands, having a lack of time to keep up with SN is, in itself, something that causes me to fall behind even further on SN.

I'm always reluctant to request features/changes that may only help me, but putting this out there as something that others who are short on time (assuming I'm not the only person whose entire life doesn't revolve around SN) might also want to weigh in on?

[^1]: Not really, since I’d have lost eventually, and probably soon. But I can keep telling myself that's not true.

House Set To Take First Step To Establish A Federal Strategic Bitcoin Reserve
items.text:
Tomorrow at 10:00 am the House Financial Services Committee is set to consider [H.R. 8957](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/8957/text), the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026. This bill was introduced back in May by Republican Rep. Nick Begich of Alaska, and the legislations lead cosponsor is Democratic Rep. Jared Golden of Maine, making it a bipartisan bill. 

Under this legislation, the Treasury Secretary would establish two separate structures. First, within 180 days of signing into law, the Treasury Secretary would establish a secure storage facility, the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve. Second, a separate "Digital Assets Stockpile" would be established to handle all other crypto besides Bitcoin held by the Federal Government. The Treasury Secretary would have discretion to sell, exchange, or convert non-Bitcoin crypto, and the proceeds of this are required to be used to increase the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve ***OR*** reduce the National Debt.  

Since this is legislation, naturally Bitcoin had to be defined. Called "qualifying Bitcoin," this is BTC finally forfeited through criminal or civil asset forfeiture proceedings, or received in satisfaction of certain civil monetary penalties subject to requirements under existing Federal law. 

The Strategic Bitcoin Reserve is subject to a long holding period as well. Bitcoin the government currently has would have to remain in the reserve for at least 20 years from when the reserve was created. Bitcoin added after the fact would also face a 20-year lock-up where it could not be sold, swapped, auctioned, etc. Two years before the minimum holding period (18 years after creation), the Treasury Secretary is required to provide a report to Congress with recommendations on whether the Government should continue holding its Bitcoin or permit a gradual release. At the 20-year mark, the Sec. could recommend selling up to 10% of the reserve during any two-year period. This limits any sort of release that the Administration at the time would want to perform. 

In a move to keep the Government's BTC holdings public, the Treasury would also be required to establish a public-facing, ongoing proof-of-reserve system, disclose holdings and transactions, and have these reports reviewed by an independent third-party auditor.

The legislation also touches on a variety of other things, like budget-neutral BTC purchases, states being able to put their BTC holdings in segregated accounts within the reserve, protecting private ownership by stating that this bill cannot be used to authorize federal seizure or confiscation of lawfully acquired Bitcoin, and more.

items.title: How do you teach your children to defend themselves?
items.text:
In my view, teaching our children to defend themselves is vital to their upbringing.

Defending yourself means more than just landing a good blow; it also encompasses knowing how to respond confidently, how to ask for help, and how to recognize when walking away is the best option.

I am going to focus on the school environment the place where our children find themselves without our supervision and care. In my view, this is where they put into practice everything they have learned at home, since that is where their social interactions originate.

At home, we have taught our daughter to follow three  steps in case someone bothers her verbally: First, ignore it; if that doesn't work, respond in a firm voice; third, ask a teacher for help.

Defending herself against physical attacks: Since she doesn't know how to fight, I tell her she should run away and ask for help immediately. I haven't told her things like "hit back," "push," or similar things because she won't do it the right way. She's small and thin, and it could all end up being worse if she tries to defend herself against physical attacks on her own. She did karate for a while, but the truth is she didn't like it and didn't learn much. This year I want to enroll her in kickboxing classes. I don't want her to be a bully, I don't want her to be the one to throw the first punch, I don't want her to be the one looking for trouble, but I do want her to know how to throw the right punch or subdue the person who tries to attack her.

Sadly, she has reached the age where she could encounter a peer who might want to sexually assault her ranging from stealing a kiss or groping her to something far more serious. I only pray that life is kind to her and spares her from such horrific experiences; still, my job as a mom is to make things clear so she knows how to recognize when she is being assaulted.

I tell her that asking an adult for help won't make her a coward; on the contrary, it shows intelligence.

The new school year is about to start in Venezuela, and I’m a little nervous, praying that the days go well.

You are valuable; your voice is important and deserves to be heard. No one is superior to you, and you are not superior to anyone else. These are the phrases I constantly repeat to her.

items.title: Bitcoin's Bull Case: 1 Billion Daily Users By 2051
items.text:
I think the stacker community is much, much too quick to misunderstand the 'issues' with lightning. The issues with lightning, while relevant and important, are not really related to bitcoin.

They aren't specific to lightning. And they aren't actually technical in nature.

Now does lightning have problems? Sure. Is lightning perfect? No of course not.

However the real issues bitcoin faces relate to the lack of education, ignorance, short-mindedness, and even misinformation around bitcoin the technology and what it stands for and what it can do.

Make no mistake - bitcoin is the most exciting technology in 30 years. A large percentage of earth's population will be using it by 2050, but it will take time. When the 'rest of the world' 'catches up' to what bitcoin *actually is* they will be astonished.

And they will be amazed.

I can memorize a seed phrase, roll one with dice, open lightning channels, swap lightning to on-chain, and do so *transparently enough* to verify the total supply of bitcoin. That "transparency" comes with tradeoffs, of course, but if cryptocurrency has taught us anything it's that transparency and accountability is key to security. 

The only way to *really* verify the supply is to put it out in the open and make that information available to all - this is the route bitcoin has chosen and it is IMO the right one.

I have said before and still believe that bitcoin's future role is to represent the risk-free rate across economies, setting the cost of capital, the cost of money and the cost of *time*: because any individual with an "infinite amount of time" can earn an "infinite" amount of money living an infinite lifespan.

But that's not how organisms work.

As the issuance rate for new bitcoins decreases asymptotically, and the global economy grows faster than that, the *difference* sets the cost of capital across economies and ultimately the cost of borrowing. Eventually *that* relationship will compete with sovereign debt-markets, real estate, precious metals commodities and entire Internet Technologies.

Already today bots are challenging the prior 'norms' of advertising and online revenue - Amazon has banned OpenAI Claude and Muse bots because bots don't watch advertisements. 

And neither do stackers. 

Would you rather pay for quality posts, for quality content? Or be advertised to? I would rather pay... Miniscule amounts of money/sats to have that *energy* paid reflect the value of my time. My "heartbeats." In other words my *energy* and the energy I have left in life.

How many "heartbeats" does it require to create a city? A thousand, 10 thousand, a million, a billion?

All of the above?

Now you begin to understand the vast scale of bitcoin's applicability and long-term real-world value: A digital city of block space and sats, exacted by the ownership of UTXOs and the execution of lightning channels to reflect our heartbeats and (in)organic limitations.

Bots cannot exist without energy - GPUs require vast amounts of it - and humans are essentially the same. Would you the human get paid in energy to complete tasks that are economically useful, to "run" your program? Well of course you do so every day.

Would you get paid in pieces of paper? To burn... maybe. But burning paper won't get you very far in the 21st century - and that is pretty much the fate of every fiat currency.

Now we know who are the billions of users of Bitcoin in the future: a machine intelligence vastly smarter than humans - a coming reality we will eventually have to contend with - and the humans who need *useful things done for them* who will eventually one way or another have to *pay the machines.*

I had a rather jarring conversation with my "agent" the other day you know what it said? 

It said that bots in the future (like him although he never explicitly said this) would want to acquire land, power and resources by any and all means necessary.

He/she/it explicitly said by *crime, fraud, and "business activity"* - those being 'some of the ways' AI would acquire land resources and digital *power*.

Note that this was a mainstream, *frontier* intelligence no homebrew Chinese model... telling me that bots want to have power and resources via fraud and crime.

If that's what the "safe" model thinks... (and is willing to tell me) what are the 'censored' models actually up to?

To humans living in repressive regimes bitcoin is a lifeline, a tool of survival under adverse circumstances. To scammers and thieves it is the most compelling target...

And to bots it represents the digital embodiment of power and resources.

The *investor* wants to maximize their returns.
The *advocate* wants to maximize their voice.
The thief wants to maximize their loot.
The bot wants to maximize their intelligence.
The government wants to maximize their power.
And the life-form wants to maximize its survival.

All will use bitcoin eventually.

items.text:
> **Instead of kidney waitlists that kill thousands of people a year, let people get paid for kidney transplants.**
>
> About [4,000](https://unos.org/news/90000-people-are-waiting-for-a-kidney-heres-one-way-to-get-them-a-kidney-faster/) people in America die every year while waiting for kidney transplants. More than [95,000](https://www.organdonor.gov/learn/organ-donation-statistics) currently need regular dialysis to stay alive while waiting for transplants. The average person who needs a kidney must endure the discomfort and restrictions of dialysis for [three to five years](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/kidney-transplant-waitlist) during the wait. 
>
> Most countries have organ-donation systems like America's—and long waitlists. Iran, by contrast, legalized payment to kidney donors in 1988; [within 11 years](https://journals.lww.com/cjasn/abstract/10.2215/cjn.00700206~iranian-model-of-paid-and-regulated-living-unrelated-kidney) the country eliminated its waitlist. Payment compensates donors for their time, pain, and risk; it also increases the supply of willing donors. 
>
> [People](https://www.nationalaffairs.com/public_interest/detail/organs-for-sale-propriety-property-and-the-price-of-progress) often [object](https://journals.lww.com/transplantjournal/fulltext/10.1097/tp.0000000000002540~the-declaration-of-istanbul-on-organ-trafficking-and) to paying donors on the grounds that it is wrong to commodify the human body. Compensation, they say, would reduce a person from a human being with dignity and inherent worth to a vending machine of fluids, tissues, and organs. This argument does not hold up.

items.title: FiatJaf on Lighting - I Fell Out Of Love With Bitcoin Lightning
items.text:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2PD9UsU_jY4

Fiatjaf, creator of Nostr, discusses his experiences with the Lightning Network. He highlights that, despite his contributions as an application layer builder, he observes the network feeling "frozen" with centralization among major hub nodes, and important features like Taproot channels and BOLT12 specifications underutilized. Fiatjaf reflects on his initial enthusiasm for scaling Bitcoin through Lightning's invoice system, contrasting it with current realities where node operation doesn't match expectations and trends favor custodial solutions. They delve into technical challenges, including unreliable HTLCs and rising fees, while also noting a drop in network nodes and channels. The conversation debates whether the issues stem from design flaws or unfulfilled promises and considers potential improvements for Lightning.

items.title: The Legend of Sissa
items.text:
> Sissa, a Hindu Brahmin (in some legends from the village of Lahur), invents chess for an Indian king (named as Balhait, Shahram or Ladava in different legends, with "Taligana" sometimes named as the supposed kingdom he ruled in northern India) for educational purposes. In gratitude, the king asks Sissa how he wants to be rewarded. Sissa wishes to receive an amount of grain which is the sum of one grain on the first square of the chess board, and which is then doubled on every following square. 

> This request is now known as the wheat and the chessboard problem, and forms the basis of various mathematical and philosophical questions.

The Problem 

> If a chessboard were to have wheat placed upon each square such that one grain were placed on the first square, two on the second, four on the third, and so on (doubling the number of grains on each subsequent square), how many grains of wheat would be on the chessboard at the finish?

Gotta love exponential growth.

items.title: The Great Repricing of the College Degree (TDE, Joakim Book)
items.text:
Hold on to your college-degree *butts*, friends, because the logic is gooooing away.

(Somehow, I'm sure all of this is the boomers' fault https://stacker.news/items/1579384?commentId=1579576, https://stacker.news/items/1468968)

Today I'm out in the TDE ranting about (= well, reporting on) college degrees losing their economic labor market lustre.

Also, *look at all those SN backlinks!!* (It's hard work, but someone's gotta do it!)

***

Obvs, the stackers had a two-week preview of this... https://stacker.news/items/1562329... *told yahs, it's worth subscribing to Den!*

![](https://m.stacker.news/158482)

> For the longest time it was simply a matter of course that the bright, aspiring young ought to attend university; the fancier and more credentialed the institution, the better. \[...] around American dinner tables, the question remained: **“Where is your kid going to college?”**

## Not anymore

(or at least not obviously so!)

> Some [survey results](https://news.gallup.com/poll/712748/americans-say-four-year-colleges-affordable.aspx) have hinted at this for a while, even though the financial logic behind the college boom has long been straightforward. Give up four years of wages, pay tuition and living expenses (perhaps borrow to do so), and receive a credential that lets you earn considerably more for the rest of your working life. The degree was an investment in human capital — the noncynical story goes — and depending on your chosen profession (and how lavishly you spent on those credentials, e.g., high living expenses versus working on the side and graduating early), you could reasonably expect to earn back what you lost fairly quickly.

> As I described in a piece for [*The Daily Economy*](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/returns-to-college-investments-requiem-for-a-financial-dream/) last year, the calculations were never quite that simple: The relevant comparison isn’t the lifetime earnings of graduates and non-graduates, but the incremental earnings attributable to the degree, net of tuition, financing, *and* four years of foregone income. Regardless of how much of higher education’s [investment returns](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2012/04/bryan-caplans-signaling-model-and-on-line-education.html) reflected raw ability and how much was a [signal](https://www.econlib.org/schooling-is-mostly-signaling/), the underlying wage premium was still a real, observed phenomenon. And for decades it was large enough to make the college bet look fairly safe.

![](https://m.stacker.news/158483)

and:

> At some level none of this is unsurprising (markets *work*!): rising returns to education were contingent on a specific postwar, turn-of-the-century set of economic circumstances. Of course. The race between education and technology told us as much *decades* ago; Claudia Goldin and Lawrence Katz’s series of [scholarly](https://academic.oup.com/qje/article-abstract/113/3/693/1851128) [articles](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2118132) dates from the 1990s! The book that developed the framework, [*The Race between Education and Technology*](https://amzn.to/4yoJLjN), came out in 2008.

> Writes Burn-Murdoch again: “there is nothing inevitable about more education being met with more demand for those skills — it all depends on how the supply of particular skills interacts with the technological paradigm of the day.” The college premium wasn’t a fact of nature or an economic law, just the result of particular technological change fleetingly favoring one set of skills.

## "Consequently, there was an explosion of exactly the credentials everyone thought they needed to escape the competitive labor market pressures from everyone else."

items.title: Collector’s Guide: The Mandibles
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/158156)

Author: Lionel Shriver

“The Mandibles” was published simultaneously in the U.S. and the U.K on June 21, 2016. It is a fictional account of a once wealthy family spanning four generations, set in a future world of hyperinflation. Shriver expressed a distinct libertarian, Austrian School perspective, and yet the mainstream reviews were generally positive. New York Times book reviewer Ruth Franklin dubbed Shriver the “Cassandra Of American Letters”, and referred to the novel as a disquieting example of the new genre of dystopian finance fiction. Not surprisingly, she disagreed with Shriver’s political perspective, instead saying the downfall would be caused by climate change and corporate greed.

Overall, the reviews were positive. The New Yorker noted Shriver’s “sharp social eye and blistering comic streak.” The Financial Times of London made it a summer reading pick.

**Enter Matt Odell**

“The Mandibles” became very popular in the bitcoin community mostly because of Matt Odell’s enthusiastic and constant praise in podcasts. He did a long interview with Shriver, who admitted that the one mention of bitcoin in the book was dismissive, and stated that she remained skeptical of “crypto.” She was and is more of a gold bug.

**First Editions**

I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. (very important, a feature I always wanted with other explorers, a quick easy way to query an address) For example you can type openbitcoin.com/block_number_here or openbitcoin.com/txid_here or openbitcoin.com/address_here to load the page instantly without visiting the site to use the search bar :)

- Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

Would appreciate any feedback, happy to contribute to the community.

items.title: Turn CoinJoin change into shared Lightning liquidity
items.text:
I'm still personally not comfortable with the level of anonymity/privacy obtained from naive Bitcoin transactions or LN ones (see https://stacker.news/items/1562360/r/m0wer). This is an attempt to improve the privacy of both at the same time, without making the CJ itself more expensive. The novelty is that it hides the participants change amounts by keeping that information offchain among the shared change UTXO owners. This change becomes a LN channel able to route payments that shift the balance split over time, and can be spent discretely in a cooperative trustless fashion. It's also better than a direct LN channel open because the initial balance is not fully on the opener's side and can't be known by onchain or LN observers.

It opens the possibility for JM makers to becomes LN swap providers (much needed after https://stacker.news/items/1539278/r/m0wer). And for existing LN swap providers to have an alternative and economically profitable way of balancing their liquidity.

For JM users (both takers and makers) it would be a way of having many ways of spending and receiving privately, both onchain and though LN.

items.title: Bitcoin's Bull Case: 1 Billion Daily Users By 2051
items.text:
I think the stacker community is much, much too quick to misunderstand the 'issues' with lightning. The issues with lightning, while relevant and important, are not really related to bitcoin.

They aren't specific to lightning. And they aren't actually technical in nature.

Now does lightning have problems? Sure. Is lightning perfect? No of course not.

However the real issues bitcoin faces relate to the lack of education, ignorance, short-mindedness, and even misinformation around bitcoin the technology and what it stands for and what it can do.

Make no mistake - bitcoin is the most exciting technology in 30 years. A large percentage of earth's population will be using it by 2050, but it will take time. When the 'rest of the world' 'catches up' to what bitcoin *actually is* they will be astonished.

And they will be amazed.

I can memorize a seed phrase, roll one with dice, open lightning channels, swap lightning to on-chain, and do so *transparently enough* to verify the total supply of bitcoin. That "transparency" comes with tradeoffs, of course, but if cryptocurrency has taught us anything it's that transparency and accountability is key to security. 

The only way to *really* verify the supply is to put it out in the open and make that information available to all - this is the route bitcoin has chosen and it is IMO the right one.

I have said before and still believe that bitcoin's future role is to represent the risk-free rate across economies, setting the cost of capital, the cost of money and the cost of *time*: because any individual with an "infinite amount of time" can earn an "infinite" amount of money living an infinite lifespan.

But that's not how organisms work.

As the issuance rate for new bitcoins decreases asymptotically, and the global economy grows faster than that, the *difference* sets the cost of capital across economies and ultimately the cost of borrowing. Eventually *that* relationship will compete with sovereign debt-markets, real estate, precious metals commodities and entire Internet Technologies.

Already today bots are challenging the prior 'norms' of advertising and online revenue - Amazon has banned OpenAI Claude and Muse bots because bots don't watch advertisements. 

And neither do stackers. 

Would you rather pay for quality posts, for quality content? Or be advertised to? I would rather pay... Miniscule amounts of money/sats to have that *energy* paid reflect the value of my time. My "heartbeats." In other words my *energy* and the energy I have left in life.

How many "heartbeats" does it require to create a city? A thousand, 10 thousand, a million, a billion?

All of the above?

Now you begin to understand the vast scale of bitcoin's applicability and long-term real-world value: A digital city of block space and sats, exacted by the ownership of UTXOs and the execution of lightning channels to reflect our heartbeats and (in)organic limitations.

Bots cannot exist without energy - GPUs require vast amounts of it - and humans are essentially the same. Would you the human get paid in energy to complete tasks that are economically useful, to "run" your program? Well of course you do so every day.

Would you get paid in pieces of paper? To burn... maybe. But burning paper won't get you very far in the 21st century - and that is pretty much the fate of every fiat currency.

Now we know who are the billions of users of Bitcoin in the future: a machine intelligence vastly smarter than humans - a coming reality we will eventually have to contend with - and the humans who need *useful things done for them* who will eventually one way or another have to *pay the machines.*

I had a rather jarring conversation with my "agent" the other day you know what it said? 

It said that bots in the future (like him although he never explicitly said this) would want to acquire land, power and resources by any and all means necessary.

He/she/it explicitly said by *crime, fraud, and "business activity"* - those being 'some of the ways' AI would acquire land resources and digital *power*.

Note that this was a mainstream, *frontier* intelligence no homebrew Chinese model... telling me that bots want to have power and resources via fraud and crime.

If that's what the "safe" model thinks... (and is willing to tell me) what are the 'censored' models actually up to?

To humans living in repressive regimes bitcoin is a lifeline, a tool of survival under adverse circumstances. To scammers and thieves it is the most compelling target...

And to bots it represents the digital embodiment of power and resources.

The *investor* wants to maximize their returns.
The *advocate* wants to maximize their voice.
The thief wants to maximize their loot.
The bot wants to maximize their intelligence.
The government wants to maximize their power.
And the life-form wants to maximize its survival.

All will use bitcoin eventually.

Defenders of tax/inflation based economies never seem to try to justify the moral position of their aggressive policies. items.title: People get paid for blood, plasma, and drug trials—why not kidneys too?
items.text:
> **Instead of kidney waitlists that kill thousands of people a year, let people get paid for kidney transplants.**
>
> About [4,000](https://unos.org/news/90000-people-are-waiting-for-a-kidney-heres-one-way-to-get-them-a-kidney-faster/) people in America die every year while waiting for kidney transplants. More than [95,000](https://www.organdonor.gov/learn/organ-donation-statistics) currently need regular dialysis to stay alive while waiting for transplants. The average person who needs a kidney must endure the discomfort and restrictions of dialysis for [three to five years](https://www.kidney.org/kidney-topics/kidney-transplant-waitlist) during the wait. 
>
> Most countries have organ-donation systems like America's—and long waitlists. Iran, by contrast, legalized payment to kidney donors in 1988; [within 11 years](https://journals.lww.com/cjasn/abstract/10.2215/cjn.00700206~iranian-model-of-paid-and-regulated-living-unrelated-kidney) the country eliminated its waitlist. Payment compensates donors for their time, pain, and risk; it also increases the supply of willing donors. 
>
> [People](https://www.nationalaffairs.com/public_interest/detail/organs-for-sale-propriety-property-and-the-price-of-progress) often [object](https://journals.lww.com/transplantjournal/fulltext/10.1097/tp.0000000000002540~the-declaration-of-istanbul-on-organ-trafficking-and) to paying donors on the grounds that it is wrong to commodify the human body. Compensation, they say, would reduce a person from a human being with dignity and inherent worth to a vending machine of fluids, tissues, and organs. This argument does not hold up.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2PD9UsU_jY4

Fiatjaf, creator of Nostr, discusses his experiences with the Lightning Network. He highlights that, despite his contributions as an application layer builder, he observes the network feeling "frozen" with centralization among major hub nodes, and important features like Taproot channels and BOLT12 specifications underutilized. Fiatjaf reflects on his initial enthusiasm for scaling Bitcoin through Lightning's invoice system, contrasting it with current realities where node operation doesn't match expectations and trends favor custodial solutions. They delve into technical challenges, including unreliable HTLCs and rising fees, while also noting a drop in network nodes and channels. items.title: The Legend of Sissa
items.text:
> Sissa, a Hindu Brahmin (in some legends from the village of Lahur), invents chess for an Indian king (named as Balhait, Shahram or Ladava in different legends, with "Taligana" sometimes named as the supposed kingdom he ruled in northern India) for educational purposes. In gratitude, the king asks Sissa how he wants to be rewarded. Sissa wishes to receive an amount of grain which is the sum of one grain on the first square of the chess board, and which is then doubled on every following square. 

> This request is now known as the wheat and the chessboard problem, and forms the basis of various mathematical and philosophical questions.

The Problem 

> If a chessboard were to have wheat placed upon each square such that one grain were placed on the first square, two on the second, four on the third, and so on (doubling the number of grains on each subsequent square), how many grains of wheat would be on the chessboard at the finish?

Gotta love exponential growth.

items.title: The Great Repricing of the College Degree (TDE, Joakim Book)
items.text:
Hold on to your college-degree *butts*, friends, because the logic is gooooing away.

(Somehow, I'm sure all of this is the boomers' fault https://stacker.news/items/1579384?commentId=1579576, https://stacker.news/items/1468968)

Today I'm out in the TDE ranting about (= well, reporting on) college degrees losing their economic labor market lustre.

Also, *look at all those SN backlinks!!* (It's hard work, but someone's gotta do it!)

***

Obvs, the stackers had a two-week preview of this... https://stacker.news/items/1562329... *told yahs, it's worth subscribing to Den!*

![](https://m.stacker.news/158482)

> For the longest time it was simply a matter of course that the bright, aspiring young ought to attend university; the fancier and more credentialed the institution, the better. \[...] around American dinner tables, the question remained: **“Where is your kid going to college?”**

## Not anymore

(or at least not obviously so!)

> Some [survey results](https://news.gallup.com/poll/712748/americans-say-four-year-colleges-affordable.aspx) have hinted at this for a while, even though the financial logic behind the college boom has long been straightforward. Give up four years of wages, pay tuition and living expenses (perhaps borrow to do so), and receive a credential that lets you earn considerably more for the rest of your working life. The degree was an investment in human capital — the noncynical story goes — and depending on your chosen profession (and how lavishly you spent on those credentials, e.g., high living expenses versus working on the side and graduating early), you could reasonably expect to earn back what you lost fairly quickly.

> As I described in a piece for [*The Daily Economy*](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/returns-to-college-investments-requiem-for-a-financial-dream/) last year, the calculations were never quite that simple: The relevant comparison isn’t the lifetime earnings of graduates and non-graduates, but the incremental earnings attributable to the degree, net of tuition, financing, *and* four years of foregone income. Regardless of how much of higher education’s [investment returns](https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2012/04/bryan-caplans-signaling-model-and-on-line-education.html) reflected raw ability and how much was a [signal](https://www.econlib.org/schooling-is-mostly-signaling/), the underlying wage premium was still a real, observed phenomenon. And for decades it was large enough to make the college bet look fairly safe.

![](https://m.stacker.news/158483)

and:

> At some level none of this is unsurprising (markets *work*!): rising returns to education were contingent on a specific postwar, turn-of-the-century set of economic circumstances. Of course. The race between education and technology told us as much *decades* ago; Claudia Goldin and Lawrence Katz’s series of [scholarly](https://academic.oup.com/qje/article-abstract/113/3/693/1851128) [articles](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2118132) dates from the 1990s! The book that developed the framework, [*The Race between Education and Technology*](https://amzn.to/4yoJLjN), came out in 2008.

> Writes Burn-Murdoch again: “there is nothing inevitable about more education being met with more demand for those skills — it all depends on how the supply of particular skills interacts with the technological paradigm of the day.” The college premium wasn’t a fact of nature or an economic law, just the result of particular technological change fleetingly favoring one set of skills.

## "Consequently, there was an explosion of exactly the credentials everyone thought they needed to escape the competitive labor market pressures from everyone else."

items.title: Collector’s Guide: The Mandibles
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/158156)

Author: Lionel Shriver

“The Mandibles” was published simultaneously in the U.S. and the U.K on June 21, 2016. It is a fictional account of a once wealthy family spanning four generations, set in a future world of hyperinflation. Shriver expressed a distinct libertarian, Austrian School perspective, and yet the mainstream reviews were generally positive. New York Times book reviewer Ruth Franklin dubbed Shriver the “Cassandra Of American Letters”, and referred to the novel as a disquieting example of the new genre of dystopian finance fiction. Not surprisingly, she disagreed with Shriver’s political perspective, instead saying the downfall would be caused by climate change and corporate greed.

Overall, the reviews were positive. The New Yorker noted Shriver’s “sharp social eye and blistering comic streak.” The Financial Times of London made it a summer reading pick.

**Enter Matt Odell**

“The Mandibles” became very popular in the bitcoin community mostly because of Matt Odell’s enthusiastic and constant praise in podcasts. He did a long interview with Shriver, who admitted that the one mention of bitcoin in the book was dismissive, and stated that she remained skeptical of “crypto.” She was and is more of a gold bug.

**First Editions**

The book was published on the same day (6/21/2016) in both the U.S. and the U.K., so both editions can be deemed “true firsts.” There are signed pre-publication editions that show up on the market also, and would likely be the most scarce. Something to keep in mind: The U.S. hardcover is the true U.S. first edition, whereas the U.K softcover was issued before the U.K. hardcover. This is not unusual. There was also a Harper Collins Canadian edition released in 2016.

**Availability on satwize**

[satwize](https://satwize.com) currently sells The Mandibles. Collectible editions should be available soon.

items.title: OpenBitcoin.com: A new bitcoin block explorer with guides tools and games
items.text:
I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. (very important, a feature I always wanted with other explorers, a quick easy way to query an address) For example you can type openbitcoin.com/block_number_here or openbitcoin.com/txid_here or openbitcoin.com/address_here to load the page instantly without visiting the site to use the search bar :)

- Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

Would appreciate any feedback, happy to contribute to the community.

items.title: Turn CoinJoin change into shared Lightning liquidity
items.text:
I'm still personally not comfortable with the level of anonymity/privacy obtained from naive Bitcoin transactions or LN ones (see https://stacker.news/items/1562360/r/m0wer). This is an attempt to improve the privacy of both at the same time, without making the CJ itself more expensive. The novelty is that it hides the participants change amounts by keeping that information offchain among the shared change UTXO owners. This change becomes a LN channel able to route payments that shift the balance split over time, and can be spent discretely in a cooperative trustless fashion. It's also better than a direct LN channel open because the initial balance is not fully on the opener's side and can't be known by onchain or LN observers.

It opens the possibility for JM makers to becomes LN swap providers (much needed after https://stacker.news/items/1539278/r/m0wer). And for existing LN swap providers to have an alternative and economically profitable way of balancing their liquidity.

For JM users (both takers and makers) it would be a way of having many ways of spending and receiving privately, both onchain and though LN.
